response.caption:
Unpopular marriage rules that we follow :)

Not saying these are the “right” rules for every marriage.
They just work really well for us. 🤍

1. We don’t do 50-50.

If you want something, you decide—and you pay for both of us.

We don’t sit there calculating who paid last time, who owes whom, or whether we’re “even.”

For us, marriage isn’t about splitting everything down the middle. It’s about taking care of each other.

2. We don’t count. We don’t keep score.

Some weeks, I’ll do all the cooking.
Other weeks, he’ll do the laundry and cook for weeks.

It depends on who has more work, who has less energy, and what life looks like that week.

We’re not competing to see who contributed more.

3. We apologise early.

If you know you were wrong, just say sorry.

There’s no prize for being the last person standing in an argument.

We’d rather apologise, talk it out and move on—unless it’s something genuinely serious or life-changing that needs a deeper conversation.

4. We keep family out of our marriage.

We love our families. But our marriage is ours.

Not every argument, disagreement or difficult phase needs to be discussed with parents, siblings or relatives.

Because once you involve everyone, you’re not just resolving an issue with your partner anymore—you’re dealing with everyone else’s opinions too.

5. We make individual plans.

Marriage shouldn’t mean losing yourself.

We have our own friends, hobbies, plans and interests—and we genuinely encourage each other to have a life outside the relationship.

You can build a life together without making your entire identity “someone’s husband” or “someone’s wife.”

Because at the end of the day, we’re not trying to win against each other.

We’re on the same team. 🤍.

media.transcript: Here's how much I spent on a two-day trip to Hong Kong Disneyland. For this video, I will be including everything from flights, hotels, and everything park-related. Starting off with the park-related expenses only, for the two-day ticket, I spent $89.50. This was a special season ticket that allowed me to go into the park two days back-to-back at a generous discount. I also did buy early park entry for my second day, which came out to $25.36. For two meals on my first day, one on my second, and a few snacks throughout the trip, I spent $58.89. This might not sound like a a lot of food to you, but that's just because I forget to eat whenever I'm at a theme park. I'm also so focused on rides and shows that meals tend to become last on my to-do list. Now for arguably the most expensive part of my trip, the merch. I must admit, the first two times I went to Hong Kong Disneyland, I wasn't a big fan of their merch game, but this time around, everything was so good. For two bag charms, one pair of ears, a postcard, a set of two mystery pins, two shirts, one hat, and two reusable bags, I spent $205.10. Yeah, I got a bit too excited. I also sold my luggage on both my arrival and departure days, which was $38.25. So on just park expenses alone, I spent $417.10. Now for travel expenses, I actually flew from Taipei and used mostly points to book my flights, so out of pocket, I only spent $60.30 on airfare round trip. For the hotel, I stayed off property at the Auberge Discovery Bay Hotel, which is about a 20-minute car ride from the park, and for one night, it was $99.05. cents. On Ubers in Hong Kong, which was four in total, I spent $69.01. And then one ride on the Disneyland Metro line, I spent $0.94. Oh, and I guess I'll include the eSIM for cellular data in Hong Kong too, which was $7.59 for the two days. So the total for trip expenses aside from the park was $236.89. And now for the grand total, including all park expenses, flights, transportation, and hotel, I spent $653.99. I definitely thought this was going to be just a cute little trip from Taipei, but the merch really got to me. But what do you think? Does this sound reasonable to you?

Deswegen wollte ich jetzt, bevor ich nur meine Entscheidung treffe, einfach mal nach eurer Meinung fragen. Ich habe mir jetzt hier meinen Laptop geschnappt und würde mir tendenziell jetzt noch ein neues Diedel bestellen. Weil quasi ist es ja jetzt umsonst. Aber nicht, dass ich eine Rechenfehler habe oder so. Deswegen dachte ich, frage ich nochmal nach eurer Meinung.

response.caption: Love doesn’t require bad bookkeeping! We can treat each other, buy gifts and be generous without relying on vibes to manage thousands of dollars in shared expenses! App we use for tracking is @Splitwise  - - -  Finaces should be based on VERIFICATION, NOT ON VIBES!

media.transcript: One thing my boyfriend and I have never ever fought about is finances because their arrangement has always been based on verification, not on vibes. For example, if I think, why am I buying all the groceries lately? I simply pull my phone, check our splitwise balance, and there it is. I'm actually behind. Never have weird fights trying to remember who paid for what. Never let their resentment build up. That balance is always a phone click away. It honestly fascinates me that so many couples fight about finances. Maybe it's because I'm an engineer, but if you can calculate it, just do it. I wish you could calculate other parts of a relationship. Like there's no database to check who's been more emotionally available. There's no pivot table for affection. There's no KPIs for being a good boyfriend. That stuff's actually challenging and you got to just figure it out. Finances are not.
